cards.front: Definition 1: how are an increasing, a decreasing and a constant function on an interval I defined?
cards.back:
Let I be an interval contained in the domain of a real valued function f. Then f is said to be
(i) increasing on I if x1 < x2 in I Þ f(x1 ) < f(x2 ) for all x1 , x2 Î I.
(ii) decreasing on I, if x 1 < x 2 in I Þ f(x 1 ) > f(x 2 ) for all x 1 , x 2 Î I.
(iii) constant on I, if f(x) = c for all x Î I, where c is a constant.
cards.quote: Let I be an interval contained in the domain of a real valued function f. Then f is said to be (i) increasing on I if x1 < x2 in I Þ f(x1 ) < f(x2 ) for all x1 , x2 Î I. (ii) decreasing on I, if x 1 < x 2 in I Þ f(x 1 ) > f(x 2 ) for all x 1 , x 2 Î I. (iii) constant on I, if f(x) = c for all x Î I, where c is a constant.

tex.back:
Let $I$ be an interval contained in the domain of a real valued function $f$. Then $f$ is said to be
(i) increasing on $I$ if $x_1 < x_2$ in $I \Rightarrow f(x_1) \le f(x_2)$ for all $x_1, x_2 \in I$.
(ii) decreasing on $I$, if $x_1 < x_2$ in $I \Rightarrow f(x_1) \ge f(x_2)$ for all $x_1, x_2 \in I$.
(iii) constant on $I$, if $f(x) = c$ for all $x \in I$, where $c$ is a constant.

cards.front: Theorem 1: when is f increasing, decreasing or constant in [a, b], in terms of f′(x)?
cards.back:
Let f be continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on the open interval (a,b). Then
(a) f is increasing in [a,b] if f ¢(x) > 0 for each x Î (a, b)
(b) f is decreasing in [a,b] if f ¢(x) < 0 for each x Î (a, b)
(c) f is a constant function in [a,b] if f ¢(x) = 0 for each x Î (a, b)
cards.quote: Theorem 1 Let f be continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on the open interval (a,b). Then (a) f is increasing in [a,b] if f ¢(x) > 0 for each x Î (a, b) (b) f is decreasing in [a,b] if f ¢(x) < 0 for each x Î (a, b) (c) f is a constant function in [a,b] if f ¢(x) = 0 for each x Î (a, b)

tex.back:
Let $f$ be continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(a, b)$. Then
(a) $f$ is increasing in $[a, b]$ if $f'(x) \ge 0$ for each $x \in (a, b)$
(b) $f$ is decreasing in $[a, b]$ if $f'(x) \le 0$ for each $x \in (a, b)$
(c) $f$ is a constant function in $[a, b]$ if $f'(x) = 0$ for each $x \in (a, b)$

cards.front: Definition 3: when does a function f have a maximum value in an interval I?

cards.back: A point c in the domain of a function f at which either f ′(c) = 0 or f is not differentiable is called a critical point of f.

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: First Derivative Test: at a critical point c, when is c a point of local maxima?
cards.back: If f ′(x) changes sign from positive to negative as x increases through c, i.e., if f ′(x) > 0 at every point sufficiently close to and to the left of c, and f ′(x) < 0 at every point sufficiently close to and to the right of c, then c is a point of local maxima.

tex.back: If $f'(x)$ changes sign from positive to negative as $x$ increases through $c$, i.e., if $f'(x) > 0$ at every point sufficiently close to and to the left of $c$, and $f'(x) < 0$ at every point sufficiently close to and to the right of $c$, then $c$ is a point of local maxima.

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: First Derivative Test: at a critical point c, when is c a point of local minima?
cards.back: If f ′(x) changes sign from negative to positive as x increases through c, i.e., if f ′(x) < 0 at every point sufficiently close to and to the left of c, and f ′(x) > 0 at every point sufficiently close to and to the right of c, then c is a point of local minima.
cards.quote: If f ′(x) changes sign from negative to positive as x increases through c, i.e., if f ′(x) < 0 at every point sufficiently close to and to the left of c, and f ′(x) > 0 at every point sufficiently close to and to the right of c, then c is a point of local minima.

tex.back: If $f'(x)$ changes sign from negative to positive as $x$ increases through $c$, i.e., if $f'(x) < 0$ at every point sufficiently close to and to the left of $c$, and $f'(x) > 0$ at every point sufficiently close to and to the right of $c$, then $c$ is a point of local minima.

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: First Derivative Test: what if the derivative does not change sign as x increases through c?
cards.back: If f ′(x) does not change sign as x increases through c, then c is neither a point of local maxima nor a point of local minima. Infact, such a point is called point of inflection.

cards.front: Second Derivative Test: when is x = c a point of local maxima?

cards.front: Second Derivative Test: when does the test fail, and what is done then?
cards.back: The test fails if f ′(c) = 0 and f ″(c) = 0. In this case, we go back to the first derivative test and find whether c is a point of local maxima, local minima or a point of inflexion.

cards.front: Working rule for the absolute maximum and minimum values of f in a closed interval [a, b], in order
cards.back:
Step 1: Find all critical points of f in the interval, i.e., find points x where either f ′(x) = 0 or f is not differentiable.
Step 2: Take the end points of the interval.
Step 3: At all these points (listed in Step 1 and 2), calculate the values of f.
Step 4: Identify the maximum and minimum values of f out of the values calculated in Step 3. This maximum value will be the absolute maximum (greatest) value of f and the minimum value will be the absolute minimum (least) value of f.

$$(b^{\gamma})^{\alpha} = b^{\gamma\alpha} = p$$
Using this in the second equation, we get

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: Define a linear programming problem.
cards.back: Thus, a Linear Programming Problem is one that is concerned with finding the optimal value (maximum or minimum value) of a linear function (called objective function) of several variables (say x and y), subject to the conditions that the variables are non-negative and satisfy a set of linear inequalities (called linear constraints).

cards.quote: A square matrix B = [bij] m × m is said to be a diagonal matrix if all its non diagonal elements are zero, that is a matrix B = [bij] m × m is said to be a diagonal matrix if bij = 0, when i ≠ j.

cards.back: A square matrix in which elements in the diagonal are all 1 and rest are all zero is called an identity matrix.
cards.quote: A square matrix in which elements in the diagonal are all 1 and rest are all zero is called an identity matrix.

cards.front: Is a scalar matrix an identity matrix, and is every identity matrix a scalar matrix?

cards.front: Formula: how is the difference A – B of two matrices of the same order defined?
cards.back:
If A = [aij], B = [bij] are two matrices of the same order, say m × n, then difference A – B is defined as a matrix D = [dij], where

tex.back:

cards.subject: mathematics

Associative Law
Existence of additive identity
The existence of additive inverse

Now A + B = [aij] + [bij] = [aij + bij]

O be an m × n zero matrix, then A + O = O

cards.front: Formula: what is the commutative law of addition for two matrices of the same order?

The distributive law
The existence of multiplicative identity

$$(A')' = A$$

They are all zero

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: What is the inverse of a square matrix A of order m?
cards.back: If A is a square matrix of order m, and if there exists another square matrix B of the same order m, such that AB = BA = I, then B is called the inverse matrix of A
cards.quote: If A is a square matrix of order m, and if there exists another square matrix B of the same order m, such that AB = BA = I, then B is called the inverse matrix of A
cards.note: A square matrix that has an inverse is called invertible.

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: How is the inverse of a square matrix A denoted, and what is A called when its inverse exists?
cards.back: If A is a square matrix of order m, and if there exists another square matrix B of the same order m, such that AB = BA = I, then B is called the inverse matrix of A and it is denoted by A– 1. In that case A is said to be invertible.
cards.quote: If A is a square matrix of order m, and if there exists another square matrix B of the same order m, such that AB = BA = I, then B is called the inverse matrix of A and it is denoted by A– 1. In that case A is said to be invertible.

tex.back: If $A$ is a square matrix of order $m$, and if there exists another square matrix $B$ of the same order $m$, such that $AB = BA = I$, then $B$ is called the inverse matrix of $A$ and it is denoted by $A^{-1}$. In that case $A$ is said to be invertible.

cards.front: Does a rectangular (non-square) matrix possess an inverse matrix?

cards.back: Inverse of a square matrix, if it exists, is unique.

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: Formula: conditional probability P(E|F) for equally likely outcomes, as a ratio of numbers of elementary events
cards.back: Number of elementary eventsfavourable to E ∩F P(E|F) = Number of elementaryevents which arefavourable to F n (E ∩ F) = n (F)
cards.quote: Number of elementary eventsfavourable to E ∩F P(E|F) = Number of elementaryevents which arefavourable to F n (E ∩ F) = n (F)

tex.back: $P(E|F) =$ (Number of elementary events favourable to $E \cap F$)/(Number of elementary events which are favourable to $F$) $= \dfrac{n(E \cap F)}{n(F)}$

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: Formula: conditional probability of E given that F has occurred (Definition 1)
cards.back:
the conditional probability of the event E given that F has occurred, i.e. P (E|F) is given by
P(E|F) = P(E F) P(F) ∩ provided P(F) ≠ 0
cards.quote: If E and F are two events associated with the same sample space of a random experiment, the conditional probability of the event E given that F has occurred, i.e. P (E|F) is given by P(E|F) = P(E F) P(F) ∩ provided P(F) ≠ 0

tex.back:
the conditional probability of the event $E$ given that $F$ has occurred, i.e. $P(E|F)$ is given by
$$P(E|F) = \frac{P(E \cap F)}{P(F)} \quad \text{provided } P(F) \neq 0$$

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: Formula: Property 1 of conditional probability, the value of P(S|F) and P(F|F)
cards.back:
Let E and F be events of a sample space S of an experiment, then we have
Property 1 P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1
cards.quote: Let E and F be events of a sample space S of an experiment, then we have Property 1 P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1

tex.back:
Let $E$ and $F$ be events of a sample space $S$ of an experiment, then we have
Property 1 $P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1$

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: Formula: Property 2 of conditional probability, P((A ∪ B)|F) for any two events A and B
cards.back:
If A and B are any two events of a sample space S and F is an event of S such that P(F) ≠ 0, then
P((A ∪ B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) – P((A ∩ B)|F)
cards.quote: If A and B are any two events of a sample space S and F is an event of S such that P(F) ≠ 0, then P((A ∪ B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) – P((A ∩ B)|F)

tex.back:
If $A$ and $B$ are any two events of a sample space $S$ and $F$ is an event of $S$ such that $P(F) \neq 0$, then

= 1 P(E ) P(A|E ) n j j j= ∑

cards.front: Formula: direction cosines of the line joining P(x₁, y₁, z₁) and Q(x₂, y₂, z₂)
cards.back:
Direction cosines of a line joining two points P(x1, y1, z1) and Q(x2, y2, z2) are
x2 − x1 , y2 − y1 , z2 − z1 PQ PQ PQ
where
PQ = ( ) (x2 − x1)2 + ( y2 − y1)2 + z2 − z1 2
cards.quote: Direction cosines of a line joining two points P(x1, y1, z1) and Q(x2, y2, z2) are x2 − x1 , y2 − y1 , z2 − z1 PQ PQ PQ where PQ = ( ) (x2 − x1)2 + ( y2 − y1)2 + z2 − z1 2

tex.back:
Direction cosines of a line joining two points $P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ are
$$\frac{x_2 - x_1}{PQ}, \quad \frac{y_2 - y_1}{PQ}, \quad \frac{z_2 - z_1}{PQ}$$

perpendicular i.e. if $\theta = 90^\circ$

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: Formula: acute angle θ between two lines with direction ratios a₁, b₁, c₁ and a₂, b₂, c₂
cards.back:
If a1, b1, c1 and a2, b2, c2 are the direction ratios of two lines and θ is the acute angle between the two lines; then
cosθ = a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 a12 + b12 + c12 a22 + b22 + c22
cards.quote: If a1, b1, c1 and a2, b2, c2 are the direction ratios of two lines and θ is the acute angle between the two lines; then cosθ = a1 a2 + b1 b2 + c1 c2 a12 + b12 + c12 a22 + b22 + c22

tex.back:
If $a_1, b_1, c_1$ and $a_2, b_2, c_2$ are the direction ratios of two lines and $\theta$ is the acute angle between the two lines; then
$$\cos\theta = \left|\frac{a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2}\,\sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2}}\right|$$

cards.front: Formula: acute angle θ between two lines with direction cosines l₁, m₁, n₁ and l₂, m₂, n₂
cards.back:
If l1 , m1 , n1 and l 2 , m2 , n2 are the direction cosines of two lines; and θ is the acute angle between the two lines; then
cosθ = |l 1 l 2 + m1m2 + n1 n2 |
cards.quote: If l1 , m1 , n1 and l 2 , m2 , n2 are the direction cosines of two lines; and θ is the acute angle between the two lines; then cosθ = |l 1 l 2 + m1m2 + n1 n2 |

tex.back:
If $l_1, m_1, n_1$ and $l_2, m_2, n_2$ are the direction cosines of two lines; and $\theta$ is the acute angle between the two lines; then
$$\cos\theta = |l_1l_2 + m_1m_2 + n_1n_2|$$

cards.quote: If θ is the acute angle between r = a1 + λ b1 and r = a2 + λ b2 , then cos θ = b1 ⋅ b2 | b1 | | b2 |

cards.front: For two parallel lines in space, what is the shortest distance between them?

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: What is meant by the shortest distance between two lines?
cards.back: By the shortest distance between two lines we mean the join of a point in one line with one point on the other line so that the length of the segment so obtained is the smallest.

cards.front: For skew lines, the line of the shortest distance will be ____ to both the lines.

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: Formula: shortest distance between the skew lines r = a₁ + λb₁ and r = a₂ + μb₂
cards.back:
Shortest distance between r = a1 + λ b1 and r = a2 + µ b2 is
(b1 × b2 ) ⋅ (a2 – a1) | b1 × b2 |
cards.quote: Shortest distance between r = a1 + λ b1 and r = a2 + µ b2 is (b1 × b2 ) ⋅ (a2 – a1) | b1 × b2 |

tex.back:
Shortest distance between $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda \vec{b}_1$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu \vec{b}_2$ is
$$\left|\frac{(\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) \cdot (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}\right|$$

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: Formula: shortest distance between two lines in Cartesian form, with direction ratios a₁, b₁, c₁ and a₂, b₂, c₂
cards.back:
The shortest distance between the lines
l1 : x − x1 a1 = y − y1 b1 = z − z1 c1 and
l2 : x − x2 a2 = y − y2 b2 = z − z2 c2
x2 − x1 y2 − y1 z2 − z1 a1 b1 c1 a2 b2 c2 is (b1c2 − b2c1 )2 + (c1a2 − c2a1 )2 + (a1b2 − a2b1 )2
cards.quote: The shortest distance between the lines l1 : x − x1 a1 = y − y1 b1 = z − z1 c1 and l2 : x − x2 a2 = y − y2 b2 = z − z2 c2 x2 − x1 y2 − y1 z2 − z1 a1 b1 c1 a2 b2 c2 is (b1c2 − b2c1 )2 + (c1a2 − c2a1 )2 + (a1b2 − a2b1 )2

tex.back:
The shortest distance between the lines
$$l_1 : \frac{x - x_1}{a_1} = \frac{y - y_1}{b_1} = \frac{z - z_1}{c_1} \quad \text{and}$$
$$l_2 : \frac{x - x_2}{a_2} = \frac{y - y_2}{b_2} = \frac{z - z_2}{c_2}$$
$$\text{is } \left|\frac{\begin{vmatrix} x_2 - x_1 & y_2 - y_1 & z_2 - z_1 \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{vmatrix}}{\sqrt{(b_1c_2 - b_2c_1)^2 + (c_1a_2 - c_2a_1)^2 + (a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)^2}}\right|$$

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: Define the shortest distance between two skew lines.
cards.back: Shortest distance between two skew lines is the line segment perpendicular to both the lines.
cards.quote: Shortest distance between two skew lines is the line segment perpendicular to both the lines.

cards.subject: mathematics
cards.front: Formula: distance between the parallel lines r = a₁ + λb and r = a₂ + μb
cards.back:
Distance between parallel lines r = a1 + λ b and r = a2 + µ b is
b × (a2 − a1) |b |
cards.quote: Distance between parallel lines r = a1 + λ b and r = a2 + µ b is b × (a2 − a1) |b |

Distance between parallel lines $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda \vec{b}$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu \vec{b}$ is
$$\left|\frac{\vec{b} \times (\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1)}{|\vec{b}|}\right|$$
